subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: 17 protons, 37 neutrons, 17 electrons
20 protons, 17 neutrons, 20 electrons
17 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons
17 protons, 20 neutrons, 17 electrons
items.note: Atomic number 17 = protons (= electrons in the atom). Neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20.

choices: The same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
The same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Different numbers of protons and electrons
The same mass number but different atomic numbers
items.note: Isotopes have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different masses.

items.stem: Which particle has a relative charge of −1 and negligible mass?
choices: Proton
Neutron
Electron
Alpha particle
items.note: Proton: +1, mass 1; neutron: 0, mass 1; electron: −1, mass ≈ 1/1836.

items.stem: How many electrons are in the ion ³²S²⁻?
items.note: Sulfur has 16 protons; a 2− charge means 2 extra electrons: 18.

items.stem: Chlorine is 75.78% ³⁵Cl (34.97) and 24.22% ³⁷Cl (36.97). Its relative atomic mass is:
Isotopes of the same element have different:
choices: Chemical properties in reactions
Numbers of electrons in their atoms
Positions in the periodic table
Physical properties such as density and rate of diffusion
items.note: Chemical properties depend on electrons; mass differences affect physical properties.

items.stem: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed that:
choices: Most of the atom's mass is in a small, positive nucleus
Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels
Atoms are solid spheres of positive charge
Neutrons are found in the nucleus
items.note: Most alpha particles passed straight through (mostly empty space); a few were deflected strongly (small dense positive nucleus).

items.stem: Boron has two isotopes, ¹⁰B (10.01) and ¹¹B (11.01). Its Ar is 10.81. What is the percentage abundance of ¹⁰B?
In a mass spectrum of an element, the peaks show:
choices: The number of electrons in each energy level
The m/z values of isotopes and their relative abundances
The energy of electrons emitted by the atoms
The number of protons in each atom
items.note: Each isotope gives a peak at its m/z (charge usually 1+); peak heights give relative abundance.

items.stem: A mass spectrum of gallium shows peaks at m/z 69 (60.1%) and 71 (39.9%). The Ar of gallium to 3 s.f. is:
A mass spectrum of chlorine gas (Cl₂) shows peaks at m/z 70, 72 and 74. The peak at 72 is due to:
choices: ³⁷Cl–³⁷Cl molecules
³⁵Cl–³⁵Cl molecules
Single ³⁶Cl atoms
³⁵Cl–³⁷Cl molecules
items.note: 35 + 37 = 72. Peaks at 70 and 74 are ³⁵Cl₂ and ³⁷Cl₂.

items.stem: Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
markscheme: Same electron configuration, which determines chemical reactions (1)
items.tactic: Chemical properties ↔ electrons; physical properties ↔ mass.

items.stem: Determine the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in ⁵⁶Fe³⁺.
items.tactic: Ions: protons fixed by the element; subtract the charge from the electron count.

items.stem: Copper has two isotopes, ⁶³Cu (62.93) and ⁶⁵Cu (64.93). Its Ar is 63.55. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
items.tactic: Set up one equation with one unknown; check the abundances add to 100%.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A mass spectrum of an invented element X shows peaks at m/z 24 (78.9%), 25 (10.0%) and 26 (11.1%).
(a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of X to 2 decimal places. (b) Suggest the identity of X using the periodic table. (c) State why a peak at m/z 12 might also appear.
markscheme: (c) Ions with a 2+ charge give m/z = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
